reading.body:
Two AI lobbying filings name Leticia Delgado, and those two filings together name eighteen separate bills.

The pattern is concentration at the filing level and breadth at the bill level. A single disclosure can list many pieces of legislation, so two filings are enough to touch eighteen bills. The client on both is the AFL-CIO, and the work runs through one lobbying firm. For AI specifically, this is what the legislative surface looks like from the inside: not one AI bill but a spread of them, tracked and reported in batches. Anyone watching AI policy through the lens of compute and power should note that the bills themselves are the input, and the buildings and grid are downstream of whatever these eighteen texts end up saying.

What the data does not cover is decisive. It gives no bill titles, no subjects, no text, no positions taken, and no spending figures. It does not say whether any of the eighteen bills concerns data centers, electricity, or AI models at all. It records that a filing named a bill, not that the bill is about AI in any substantive sense. The count of two filings is also small, so this is one lobbyist's slice of a much larger record, not a measure of the sector.

The page draws no conclusion about the person, and neither should the reader. The useful fact is structural: AI lobbying disclosure is granular enough to name individual bills, which means the legislative pipeline around AI can be counted, and counting it is the first step to seeing where the constraint on compute will actually be set.
